you gave me 2 reports. this last one here. And then there was a report you gave me before: <first-report> Priority roadmap P0 — Release-blocking hardening ### 1. Fix concurrent smooth-turn persistence Evidence: root npm test fails on: ```text isolated smooth-turn writers retry instead of clobbering stale whole-snapshot state ``` Relevant code: - src/thread/async-thread/services/smooth-turn-service.ts - src/thread/store/file-thread-store.ts - tests/thread/smooth-turn-service.test.ts Why it matters: this is exactly the kind of bug that corrupts or drops derived state during real dogfooding, especially with background maintenance, user-prompt smoothing, and smart-compact catch-up overlapping. Suggested direction: - Introduce a narrow store operation such as updateTurnDerivedState(threadId, turnId, expectedSourceRevision, patchFn). - Avoid rewriting entire turns.json from a stale whole-snapshot when only one turn’s smooth state changes. - Keep source revision and message watermark checks strict, but make turns-revision conflicts naturally mergeable for disjoint turn updates. ### 2. Establish CI before further feature work Minimum CI: ```sh npm run typecheck npm test npm --prefix packages/lh-context run typecheck npm --prefix packages/lh-context test npm --prefix packages/lh-context run build ``` Optional/nightly: ```sh npm run test:e2e ``` This codebase has too many subtle invariants to proceed without automated gates. ### 3. Freeze current schema contracts Before large refactors, write a current-state schema/readme for: - .context-steward/threads/<id>/thread.json - messages.jsonl - turns.json - chunks.json - projection revisions - generated PI session metadata entries This will protect packaging, migration, and future agents. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── P1 — Architectural seam cleanup ### 4. Split the PI extension monolith src/context-steward/pi/pi-extension.ts currently owns: - event capture; - active session reconciliation; - stale PI context fallback; - prompt-visible tool-result projection; - background maintenance scheduling; - command registration; - command formatting; - smart compact session switching; - timing logs. That file is now an integration subsystem, not a file. Suggested split: ```text src/context-steward/pi/ extension.ts # thin composition root event-capture-adapter.ts active-session-coordinator.ts command-registration.ts command-handlers.ts background-maintenance-scheduler.ts prompt-projection-coordinator.ts pi-context-snapshot.ts pi-notifications.ts ``` Do not change behavior first. Extract with tests green after each step. ### 5. Declare canonical module names and retire alias namespaces gradually There are many one-line re-export shims: - src/context-steward/domain/* → src/thread/domain/* - src/context-steward/services/* → src/thread/services/* - src/context-workbench/* → src/workbench / src/thread-view This is understandable historical rename debt, but it creates two vocabularies. Pick the durable public names. My recommendation: - Keep Context Steward as product/system name. - Use thread for canonical source domain. - Use thread-view for projection/view IR. - Use workbench for inspection/query surface. - Mark context-steward/* and context-workbench/* as compatibility import paths. - Add a lint/grep guard preventing new internal imports from compatibility shims. ### 6. Extract shared band allocation/readiness policy Selection/readiness logic appears in: - src/thread/async-thread/services/async-thread-run-service.ts - src/thread-view/services/thread-view-builder.ts - src/commands/smart-compact.ts - src/workbench/services/workbench-query-service.ts Risk: prepare/readiness can say one set of artifacts is needed while builder/compact selects differently. Create a shared module like: ```text src/thread-view/policy/ band-budget-policy.ts source-unit-selection-policy.ts artifact-readiness-policy.ts token-count-readiness-policy.ts ``` Inputs should be immutable snapshots; outputs should be explainable plans: ```ts interface ProjectionSelectionPlan { fullFidelityTurnIds: Set<string>; smoothTurnIds: Set<string>; detailedChunkIds: Set<string>; briefChunkIds: Set<string>; blockers: StewardIssue[]; accountingDecisions: ... } ``` Then async prepare, smart compact, Thread View builder, and workbench reports consume the same plan. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── P2 — Store and maintenance hardening ### 7. Break up FileThreadStore FileThreadStore currently handles: - thread CRUD; - actor/message/turn/chunk writes; - root index reconciliation; - threadId map; - generated rollout identity migration; - legacy rollout retirement; - file locking; - fixture creation; - atomic file helpers. This makes every storage change high-risk. Suggested decomposition: ```text thread-file-layout.ts atomic-json-store.ts thread-mutation-lock.ts thread-index-store.ts target-identity-map-store.ts thread-record-store.ts message-log-store.ts turn-state-store.ts chunk-state-store.ts projection-revision-store.ts legacy-rollout-migrator.ts fixture-store.ts ``` Keep the public ThreadStore interface stable while carving internals. ### 8. Introduce first-class durable jobs or maintenance records The architecture/PRD expected visible jobs. Current implementation often encodes work state in derived records plus in-memory scheduling: - backgroundMaintenanceByThreadId in PI extension; - inFlight sets in lower-band/user-prompt services; - debug logs under .context-steward/debug. That is okay for pre-MVP, but brittle across restart/process boundaries. Recommended next model: ```ts MaintenanceJob { jobId; threadId; kind: "smooth_turn" | "user_prompt_smoothing" | "chunk_transcript" | "lower_band_detailed" | ... sourceRevision; targetId; status: "queued" | "running" | "succeeded" | "failed" | "cancelled"; attempts; provider/model; lastError; createdAt/updatedAt; } ``` You do not need a full worker system immediately. Even persisted “recent job attempt” records would improve inspectability and restart behavior. ### 9. Standardize Result vs exception boundaries The codebase has a good StewardResult pattern, but also throws StewardResultError in service APIs. That is workable, but the boundary is inconsistent. Recommendation: - Domain/store/policy functions return StewardResult. - Top-level command/event adapters catch and convert to user-visible notifications. - Model-provider adapters may throw provider-specific errors internally, but service wrappers convert to StewardIssue. This will simplify command handlers and background maintenance failure behavior. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── P3 — Legacy cleanup and product polish ### 10. Quarantine or delete placeholder-era generation src/thread/async-thread/services/placeholder-artifact-service.ts appears production-unused except fixtures/helpers. New code correctly treats semantic lower-band artifacts as authoritative and blocks legacy placeholder chunks. Action: - Move placeholder generation to src/thread/async-thread/legacy/ or tests. - Keep read compatibility for old chunks. - Prevent any normal production path from creating placeholder lower-band artifacts. - Eventually migrate old fixtures/snapshots and delete generation code. This will reduce confusion around “placeholder,” “semantic,” “detailed,” and “brief.” ### 11. Make packages/lh-context consume typed read models The package is valuable, but currently uses a lot of any and direct file-shape knowledge: - packages/lh-context/src/core/io.ts - packages/lh-context/src/core/inspectors.ts - packages/lh-context/src/core/util.ts That is acceptable for a first CLI slice, but it will drift. Options: 1. Export read-only schema/types from root source into the package build. 2. Create a small shared package for persisted record codecs. 3. Add runtime validation with lightweight guards before producing reports. Also note: package build bundles extension from ../../src/context-steward/pi/pi-extension.ts. That couples the package to repo internals. For publishing, expose a stable package-owned entrypoint. ### 12. Add root hygiene Observed noise/risk: - tracked .thread-snapshots/* files; - runtime/session artifacts near source; - .beads modified during work; - package .pi/ untracked during package work; - docs from older PI versions still present. Recommendations: - Decide whether .thread-snapshots is source artifact or local runtime artifact. If local, ignore it. - Add engines to root package.json matching package Node requirement. - Add “current-state” docs separate from historical epics. - Keep generated package dist/ ignored, but document publish build flow. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Major technical debt buckets 1. Orchestration files are too large Largest production files: ```text 2625 src/context-steward/pi/pi-extension.ts 2255 src/thread/async-thread/services/async-thread-run-service.ts 2146 src/thread/store/file-thread-store.ts 1244 src/thread-view/services/thread-view-builder.ts 980 src/workbench/services/workbench-query-service.ts 969 src/thread/async-thread/services/smooth-turn-service.ts 941 src/thread/async-thread/services/lower-band-compression-service.ts ``` These are not merely long; they contain multiple policy layers. That makes changes hard for agents and humans because local reasoning is insufficient. Refactor principle: extract policies before extracting utilities. Good target abstractions: - selection plan; - readiness report; - mutation transaction; - model-provider attempt policy; - generated output accounting; - PI session replacement coordinator. 2. Concurrency and persistence are the biggest correctness risk Good existing pieces: - source revisions; - message high-watermarks; - turns revisions; - file mutation leases; - process-local queues; - stale write tests. Remaining risk: - services still build whole-snapshot writes; - retry logic is scattered; - some in-flight guards are process-local; - background maintenance is not durable; - current test failure proves a race still exists. Priority: fix this before adding major new behavior. 3. Policy duplication across prepare/build/inspect The system has several consumers that need to answer: - Which turns/chunks will be selected? - Which artifacts are required? - Which token counts are trusted? - Which missing states are blockers vs degraded warnings? - Which lower-band chunks are eligible? Right now these answers are distributed. This is a classic pre-MVP debt pattern: correctness exists in tests, but policy is not centralized. Centralizing this will make the codebase more maintainable than almost any cosmetic cleanup. 4. Historical naming drift The domain language evolved: - Context Steward → thread - Context Workbench → workbench/thread-view - placeholder lower-band → semantic lower-band - projection/thread-view/generated rollout terms overlap The architecture docs are directionally strong, but some concrete versions are stale. The code also preserves old import paths. This is manageable, but it needs a deliberate naming freeze. 5. Legacy placeholder state still taxes cognition The current semantic lower-band direction is right. But the code still has a lot of placeholder-era accommodation. This is okay for compatibility, but production generation paths should not include placeholder concepts anymore. Keep legacy read support; remove or quarantine legacy write support. 6. Observability is useful but ad hoc There are good status commands and debug logs, but operational telemetry is spread across: - timing logs; - command outputs; - status inspection services; - derived state fields; - console stderr warnings; - package CLI reports. A small unified operational event log would help: ```text .context-steward/threads/<id>/events.jsonl ``` Events: - capture succeeded/failed; - smoothing scheduled/succeeded/failed; - lower-band generation attempts; - compact started/blocked/written/reloaded; - prompt projection truncation applied; - token count provider failures. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── What I would not change first I would not rewrite the whole architecture. The core model is good. I would also avoid these early: - migrating from file storage to database; - changing turn/chunk band </first-report> I liked the first report better. any idea why that might be?

- P1 architectural seam cleanup:
  - Split `src/context-steward/pi/pi-extension.ts`, which had become an integration subsystem handling event capture, session reconciliation, prompt projection, maintenance scheduling, command registration/formatting, smart compact, and timing logs. Proposed decomposition into a thin composition root plus coordinators/adapters.
  - Pick canonical module/domain names and gradually retire alias namespaces. Recommendation: keep “Context Steward” as product name, but use `thread`, `thread-view`, and `workbench` as canonical source/module vocabulary, with old import paths treated as compatibility shims and blocked for new internal use.
  - Centralize band selection/readiness/token-budget policy, which was duplicated across async-thread run service, thread-view builder, smart compact, and workbench query service. Suggested shared policy modules returning an explainable immutable `ProjectionSelectionPlan`.

- P2 store and maintenance hardening:

- Orchestration files are too large and combine multiple policy layers (`pi-extension.ts`, `async-thread-run-service.ts`, `file-thread-store.ts`, `thread-view-builder.ts`, etc.).

- Historical naming drift creates two vocabularies.
- Legacy placeholder lower-band support still imposes cognitive overhead.

- Oversized orchestration files/monoliths.

- Legacy placeholder lower-band concepts still add cognitive load.
- Observability exists but is ad hoc; a unified operational event log was suggested.

Explicit “don’t do first” guidance:
- Don’t rewrite the whole architecture.
- Don’t migrate from file storage to a database yet.
- Don’t change the core turn/chunk band model early.

detailed:
Core conclusion: the architecture is faster because compaction is mostly precomputed during normal message/turn flow, not during the compact itself. The canonical store becomes a prepared substrate: raw messages are canonical; turns, smooth turns, chunks, brief/detailed artifacts, token counts, provenance, and readiness state are all derived and kept up to date. Smart compact then mostly reads canonical + derived state, selects bands, renders the rollout file, and switches PI.

Main tradeoff: this shifts complexity into normal operation, especially concurrency and asynchronous maintenance. The design should therefore treat capture as the critical path and keep it simple/strict/fast, while everything derived is async, transactional, retryable, and allowed to lag. Key principles: capture always wins; derived artifacts are disposable; commits should be small; every artifact needs an explicit source revision/hash; maintenance must be inspectable; backpressure must protect live interaction.

The sharpest risk is not derived text generation itself, but overlap at message-end when tool-result trimming happens at the same time as canonical ingest, token accounting, and derived maintenance. The needed separation is:

- Canonical ingest surface: store the full raw message/tool result transactionally and idempotently; no trimming, no model calls, no summarization.
- Prompt-visible trim surface: a non-canonical projection for PI pressure, with policy and original hash/ref recorded.
- Derived maintenance surface: generate smoothing/chunking/lower-band artifacts only from finalized canonical storage, never from a live-trimmed prompt view.

Invariant: any derived artifact must record the canonical source revision/content hash it came from. If canonical capture is not finalized, derived work should wait, retry, or be marked blocked. SQLite fits this well because it can make message-end a small transaction: persist raw content and metadata, mark capture complete, enqueue maintenance jobs, and keep trimming as a separate projection step.
brief:
- Core insight: keep canonical messages/turns plus precomputed derived artifacts continuously up to date, so smart compact just selects/renders from prepared state instead of summarizing a huge prompt on demand.
- This trades compact-time cost for more concurrency in normal operation; derived work must be async, transactional, retryable, stale-tolerant, and allowed to lag.
- Key rule: raw/canonical capture is the critical path and must stay simple/fast; derived artifacts are disposable, small-commit, revision-tagged, and inspectable.
- Main unresolved risk is message-end overlap with tool-result trimming: canonical ingest, prompt-visible trimming, and derived maintenance must be separate.
- Required invariant: full raw tool result/message is persisted before any trim-based projection affects downstream work; derived artifacts must reference canonical source revision/hash, not live-trimmed prompt text.
- SQLite still looks like the right foundation for small transactional ingest + job enqueue + separate trimming projection.

{"text":"Yes — there are real advantages to keeping banding **turn-based** rather than message-based.

## Advantages of turn-based banding

### 1. Turns preserve task intent

A turn usually means:

```text
user asks thing -> agent reasons/acts/tools/responds
```

That is a meaningful unit. If banding splits by individual messages, you can easily keep:

```text
tool result
assistant answer
```

but lose:

```text
original user request
tool call that produced result
```

Turn-based selection keeps the causal bundle together.

### 2. Cleaner summaries

Smoothing a whole turn is much easier than smoothing arbitrary messages.

A turn has:

- initiating prompt
- agent response
- tool calls
- tool results
- final answer / stop reason

That gives the smoothing/compression model enough structure to produce useful context.

### 3. Easier source mapping

Turn-based banding makes provenance simpler:

```text
smooth turn X came from turn X
chunk Y came from source range A-B
```

Message-based projection creates messier provenance:

```text
these 37 messages from 12 turns were kept, these 8 were dropped, these 4 were transformed
```

Much harder to audit.

### 4. Better semantic continuity

A coding task often spans a whole prompt cycle. Splitting inside that cycle can create incoherent compacted context.

For example, keeping a test failure but dropping the command that caused it can confuse the next model call.

### 5. More stable chunking

Chunks are built from closed turns. If banding starts operating at message granularity, chunk boundaries become less stable and harder to reason about.

Turn-based chunks give you a stable history lattice:

```text
turns -> chunks -> detailed/brief summaries
```

That is much easier to cache, invalidate, and regenerate.

### 6. Less policy complexity

Message-based banding would need many special cases:

- keep user messages?
- keep assistant final text?
- keep reasoning?
- keep tool calls but truncate results?
- preserve call/result pairs?
- what about failed tools?
- what about multiple tool calls in one assistant response?

Turn-based banding avoids most of that.

## But turn-based banding has a weakness

It assumes a turn is a manageable unit.

That breaks when one turn contains:

```text
150 tool calls
300k tokens
```

At that point, the turn is too large to be a safe indivisible projection unit.

That is why the live tool-result truncation pressure valve is useful. It handles pathological message-level bloat without making the whole banding architecture message-based.

## How easy is the current banding system to reason about?

Conceptually: **pretty easy**.

It has a clean model:

```text
newest -> raw full fidelity
then -> smooth turns
then -> detailed chunks
oldest -> brief chunks
```

That is understandable.

Architecturally: **moderately easy**.

The source units are mostly clear:

```text
turns for upper bands
chunks for lower bands
```

The ordering principle is clear:

```text
newest/highest fidelity backward
```

The generated result has auditable band metadata.

- token count trust/source policies
- stale token counts
- blocker/degraded issues

- chunk readiness
- lower-band artifact availability
- legacy placeholder chunks
- active/draft/archived thread views
- exact final generated-session recount
- reduction retries

implementation complexity: 6/10 approachable

Turn-based banding was reaffirmed as the core architecture because it preserves semantic bundles: user intent, agent reasoning, tool calls/results, and final response stay together. This makes summaries cleaner, provenance easier to audit, semantic continuity better for coding tasks, and chunk boundaries more stable. It also avoids the policy and bookkeeping explosion that message-level banding would create (keep/drop/truncate rules for every message type, call/result pairing, failed tools, multi-tool assistant turns, etc.).

The main weakness of a strictly turn-based system is pathological turn size: a single turn can contain huge tool-result volume and blow context before it is eligible for normal smoothing/chunking/banding. The solution is live tool-result truncation as a message-level “pressure valve” or emergency local relief, so the system can off-gas context pressure without abandoning the turn/chunk abstraction. This preserves the source-of-truth rule: canonical stored history remains full fidelity, while the prompt-visible version may be truncated.

Overall reasoning about the banding system was described as fairly easy at the conceptual level and still reasonably inspectable in practice because it follows a clean fidelity ladder: newest/full detail → smooth turns → detailed chunks → brief chunks. But implementation is nontrivial due to token-count trust and staleness, degraded/blocker handling, strict vs prepare modes, chunk readiness, lower-band artifact availability, legacy placeholders, active/draft/archived views, exact recounting, retries, and prompt-visible truncation logic. The key open constraint is balancing turn-based simplicity against rare but extreme message-level spikes, which truncation is meant to solve without making the whole system message-based.
brief:
Turn-based banding is preferred over message-based banding because it preserves task intent, keeps provenance/auditability simpler, and makes chunk/smoothing behavior more stable and understandable. Message-level handling is only needed as a local pressure valve for pathological cases (e.g. huge tool outputs) so the core architecture can stay `turns -> chunks -> bands`. Live tool-result truncation should handle those spikes without changing the source-of-truth rule: full canonical storage, truncated prompt view.

Current banding is conceptually clean and mostly turn/chunk based, but implementation is moderately complex due to token-count trust, stale counts, strict/prepare modes, chunk readiness, legacy placeholders, view states, retries, and prompt-visible truncation.

Observed context behavior (rising to ~18–19%, then dropping to ~12–14%, then smaller per-turn deltas) was judged consistent with live tool-result truncation. {"text":"It’s a high-level summary plus the major architectural details I still have available. More comprehensively, from memory:

## Product purpose

PI Long Horizon is a long-horizon coding-agent harness built on PI. It exists because raw chat transcripts eventually become unusable as coding sessions grow. The product aims to let sessions continue coherently past one context window by maintaining a managed memory substrate.

The v1 goal was dogfooding a manual loop:

```text
capture session -> maintain derived memory -> inspect state -> smart compact -> continue in generated PI session
```

It was not trying to fully automate all memory management initially. Manual smart compact and visible operator state were important.

## Key glossary/domain terms

I remember these terms:

- **Thread**: canonical durable session.
- **Canonical Thread**: full-fidelity source truth.
- **Message**: typed captured unit from PI.
- **Message part**: structured subcontent inside a message.
- **Turn**: prompt-bounded unit, usually user prompt plus assistant/tool activity until next prompt.
- **Closed turn**: turn complete enough for smoothing/chunking/projection.
- **Smooth turn**: compressed turn-level representation.
- **Chunk**: group of closed turns for lower-band compression.
- **Band**: fidelity region in generated context.
- **Projection**: derived selection/rendering from canonical thread into PI-compatible session.
- **Generated session**: compacted PI session file emitted by the system.
- **Smart compact**: manual operation to create/load a generated session.
- **Maintenance state**: async processing status, blockers, degraded modes.
- **Import/attach**: bring an existing PI session under management.

## Core product principles

The docs emphasized:

1. **Preserve full source truth.**
 Generated compacted sessions must not replace the canonical thread.

2. **Make compaction inspectable.**
 Operators should know what is captured, smoothed, chunked, blocked, stale, or degraded.

3. **Prefer explicit degraded/blocker states over silent failure.**
 If summaries/counts/artifacts are missing or stale, the system should expose that.

4. **Use semantic units.**
 Turns and chunks are meaningful units for memory, better than arbitrary transcript slicing.

5. **Generated output is disposable.**
 It is a projection/revision, not the durable record.

6. **Start with manual smart compact.**
 The PRD was v1/dogfood-oriented, not promising magical always-on compaction.

## The planned memory model

The planned context model was stratified by age/fidelity.

Newest context should be closest to raw transcript. Older context should be progressively compressed.

The four bands I remember:

```text
full fidelity / raw recent turns
smooth turns
detailed chunk summaries
brief chunk summaries
```

The idea was to pack a generated context from newest to oldest while respecting a budget. The generated session should contain enough high-fidelity recent context for immediate work and enough compressed old context to maintain continuity.

## Turns

Turns were central.

A turn is prompt-bounded. A user prompt begins a turn. Assistant messages and tool results following that prompt belong to the same turn until the next prompt.

Closed turns are eligible for derived processing:

- smoothing
- chunk membership
- projection decisions

There was also a need to repair turns, because sessions imported from PI or captured around extension startup may have incomplete/incorrect turn boundaries.

## Smoothing

Smooth turns are per-turn compressed representations.

My memory is that smoothing was meant to preserve:

- user intent
- decisions made
- files touched
- important facts/results
- unresolved follow-ups

while dropping verbose raw details.

The PRD/arch treated this as an async maintenance process, not something blocking every user turn.

## Chunking and lower bands

Chunks group older closed turns into larger units.

The lower bands use chunk-level summaries:

- detailed summary: richer compressed history
- brief summary: very compact older history

Chunks allow the system to avoid needing every individual old turn in the generated context.

The docs expected chunking/summarization readiness to matter. If artifacts were missing, the projection might block/degrade rather than pretend everything is fine.

## Smart compact flow

Manual smart compact was a major v1 operator action.

The intended flow:

1. Capture canonical session state.
2. Ensure turns are closed/repaired enough.
3. Ensure needed async artifacts exist or report blockers.
4. Build a projection/thread view from canonical thread and artifacts.
5. Allocate context across bands.
6. Emit a generated PI session file.
7. Have PI load/switch to that generated session.
8. Record projection revision/metadata.

The generated session should include enough metadata to trace what canonical source revision and projection revision it came from.

## Attach/import

The system needed to manage both fresh sessions and existing PI sessions.

Attach/import means:

- read an existing PI session file
- create a canonical thread from it
- infer turns
- maybe repair incomplete boundaries
- start managing future messages

The docs cared about not losing pre-extension session history.

## PI extension role

The PI extension/adaptor was supposed to be relatively thin but crucial:

- observe PI lifecycle/session events
- capture user/assistant/tool messages
- run commands
- expose status
- trigger smart compact
- cause PI to reload generated sessions

The extension should not become the canonical business model itself. The canonical thread/domain layer owns truth.

## Storage

The architecture was local/file-backed.

I remember a file-backed thread store, likely JSON records, with directories under something like `.context-steward` or similar.

The architecture valued local durability and inspectability.

## Async maintenance

The system has background/async maintenance concepts:

- close turns
- smooth turns
- chunk turns
- generate summaries
- update readiness state
- expose blockers

It should tolerate partial readiness. Not every artifact may be available immediately.

## Degraded/blocker state

The docs seemed to emphasize visible failure modes.

Examples of conditions that should be visible:

- turn repair needed
- smoothing failed/stale
- chunking unavailable
- summary artifacts missing
- token counts missing/stale
- generated projection cannot be trusted
- PI session not managed or not on latest rollout

This is important because a memory system silently dropping or inventing context is dangerous.

## Token budgeting

The PRD obviously discussed context windows and budgets, but my memory is that exact token-accounting implementation was less detailed in the docs than in the code.

The docs wanted projection to fit a target context size. It probably described target model context, reserved budget, and choosing bands under a token budget.

But the implemented provider-backed count policy was more advanced than the docs.

## Projection/compiler

The tech architecture described a compiler-like layer:

```text
canonical thread + derived artifacts + budget policy
 -> generated PI-compatible session
```

This was important because future target formats could exist. PI was the first target.

The projection layer should be deterministic/traceable enough to inspect what got included and why.

## Generated sessions and revisions

Generated PI sessions were planned as real session files that PI could load.

There was metadata around projection revision / source revision so the system could tell:

- what generated file came from what canonical source
- whether the active PI session is generated
- whether it is latest
- whether capture after compaction continues from canonical source

## Architecture boundaries

The architecture separated:

```text
domain records
file store
capture/import services
async maintenance services
projection services
PI target writer
PI extension commands/events
```

This separation was a big part of the design.

## What was planned vs later implementation

Planned:

- canonical thread
- message/part records
- prompt-bounded turns
- async smoothing
- chunks
- detailed/brief summaries
- stratified bands
- manual smart compact
- generated PI sessions
- attach/import
- visible status/blockers

Less planned or more mature in code:

- exact provider token counting
- generated-session final count enforcement
- smart compact reduction loop
- thread-view as major IR
- active prompt projection
- rich workbench reports
- fixture/eval tooling
- generated rollout reconciliation
- mutation leasing/concurrency guard
- prompt-visible tool-result truncation

## Overall remembered conclusion

My overall conclusion was:

The initial plan was ambitious but coherent. The implementation largely matched it and in several areas exceeded it. It did not feel like a random evolved codebase; it felt like the planned domain model survived contact with implementation.

The biggest architectural success was preserving this distinction:

```text
canonical source truth != prompt-visible/generated projection
```

The biggest practical addition was message-level tool-result off-gassing, because it handles context pressure that turn/chunk banding cannot handle, especially huge live tool output inside a current/recent turn.

The biggest conceptual clarification from our discussion was that band allocation numbers are not exact targets. They are heuristic shaping parameters for the selection process. ## `ls-epic` approach

The best part is that it makes the epic an **execution contract**, not just a requirements document.

The chain is clear:

```text
User / workflow
 -> flows
 -> ACs
 -> TCs
 -> data contracts
 -> tech design questions
 -> story breakdown
```

That gives downstream agents much less room to invent.

The approach is especially good for AI work because it fights common AI failure modes:

- vague requirements becoming confident implementation
- hidden scope expansion
- context-history dependence
- weak test mapping
- tech design decisions leaking into functional spec
- story slicing without AC coverage proof

The strongest pieces are:

- ACs and TCs co-located
- data contracts allowed, but stack-neutral
- tech design questions formalized instead of buried
- story breakdown maps back to ACs
- validation prompt forces traceability review
- context economics explicitly explains why artifact handoff matters

I also like that it is not anti-detail. It is anti-wrong-detail. It allows precision where precision belongs.

## Epic 1 as an example

Epic 1 is a very good example.

It took PRD Feature 1 and expanded it into a complete functional substrate spec:

- canonical Thread
- actors
- messages
- typed parts
- prompt-bounded turns
- generated PI target metadata
- attach/import
- repair readiness
- real-session fixtures

canonical source Thread is source truth;
PI session/generated file is target/runtime output.

- duplicate events
- unsupported schema
- append failure
- pre-turn records
- branch import ambiguity
- incomplete turn reconstruction
- stale repair input
- fixture creation failure

The story breakdown was also excellent because the implementation commits followed it almost exactly.

That is unusually strong evidence that the epic was not merely well-written — it was operationally useful.

Epic 1 is large. The skill warns that 5+ flows / 800+ lines creates downstream pressure, and Epic 1 did. The closeout review found cross-story integration issues.

But that does not mean the epic failed. It means the skill’s warning was accurate.

The closeout review caught:

- attach/import lifecycle issue
- active branch context issue
- missing real integration gate

```text
ls-epic methodology: excellent for agentic implementation reliability
Epic 1: strong, realistic example with real-world complexity
Implementation trace: validates the approach
```

- Artifact acceptance can diverge from committed repo truth. Story 02 artifacts reportedly claimed `.pi/extensions/context-steward.ts` existed, but git history suggested it did not land in the Story 02 commit and appeared later in commit `39dd08d` for the PI CLI E2E gate. This implies verification may have passed against a richer workspace than what was durably committed. Proposed fix: final-package changed files must be compared against staged/committed files, possibly via a generated commit manifest; acceptance should fail if a claimed production file is absent from the commit.

- Early integration gates were too weak. `verify-all` could pass while integration tests were absent, making the gate sound stronger than it was. This was especially risky for Story 02, where runtime wiring was the core risk. Later hardening added `.pi/extensions/context-steward.ts`, `test:e2e`, `e2e-cli.e2e.test.ts`, and a stronger `verify-all` including verify, integration, and E2E. Proposed refinement: gates that claim integration/E2E coverage should fail or explicitly record an accepted risk when zero tests are discovered.

- Identity and association logic remains dangerous. Story 01 exposed cases where a session known first by `sessionFilePath` and later by `sessionId` could create duplicate canonical threads; fuzzy fallback by `cwd` or generated path could merge distinct PI sessions; and failed reassociation could still mutate disk. Proposed checklist for identity/store stories: same cwd with different sessions must remain separate, same session with different identifiers must resolve to one thread, failed reassociation must not mutate disk, duplicate replay must be idempotent, and fuzzy association must be disallowed unless explicitly specified.

- File-backed persistence needs standard failure-injection coverage. Story 01 risks included partial thread directories after failed creation, metadata corruption during atomic rewrites, and cross-instance rename races because per-instance queues did not protect multiple `FileThreadStore` instances. Proposed tests: fail before write, during temp write, during rename, after append, restart/index rebuild, and concurrent mutation from multiple store instances.

- Concurrency/source-order bugs are subtle but critical. Example: append A is invoked before append B, but A blocks on actor declaration while B reaches the queue first, so B receives an earlier `sourceOrder`. This corrupts canonical chronology used by repair, smoothing, chunking, and projection. Proposed tests should prove invocation order is preserved despite actor creation, duplicate checks, or turn-writer delays.

- Specs often already contained the right warnings, but implementors did not consistently internalize them. Story 02’s anti-shim requirements implied proving the real production capture path, yet the first implementation focused on helpers/services. Story 01 centered target-key identity, yet unsafe fallback matching still appeared. Proposed refinement: before coding, generate a “must-prove edge checklist” from anti-shim requirements, NTC tests, design risks, and open questions, then require each item to map to concrete files/tests.

- Runtime contract uncertainty should be tracked explicitly. Story 02 still had an open question around whether live `message_end` events expose stable identifiers such as session entry IDs, response IDs, or tool call IDs. If not, fallback fingerprinting risks either duplicate appends or false suppression. Proposed table: assumed PI contract, validated PI contract, fallback behavior, risk, and dogfood/manual evidence.

- Logs/receipts can drift from artifact truth. Example: Story 01 team log implied `008-verify` was final pass, while artifacts showed `008-verify` was revise and `010-verify` was the actual pass. Proposed fix: generate team-log receipts from final package artifacts rather than manually maintaining them.

- Test confidence levels should be explicit. Fake extension API tests can prove registration works if imported/invoked, but not that PI CLI loads `.pi/extensions/context-steward.ts`. Proposed labels: unit, service integration, fake runtime integration, real runtime E2E, and dogfood/manual; story acceptance should require the appropriate level for the story type.

Overall direction: the specs are not the main problem. The weak spots are boundary proofs. The process should add concrete gates/checklists for production-path proof, committed-artifact proof, nonzero meaningful integration/E2E coverage, and identity/persistence/concurrency hardening. Open follow-ups include validating Story 02’s live PI event identifiers, deciding whether zero-test integration gates hard-fail, and automating manifests/receipts to reduce audit drift.

Review of Story 02 artifacts surfaced broader process issues across Stories 00–02:

- Biggest recurring gap: service code/tests can pass without proving the real production/runtime path. For PI/runtime stories, require explicit proof that the actual extension/entrypoint exists, is committed, is loaded by PI, registers the right handlers/events, and uses real default deps; add smoke/E2E where possible.
- Artifact truth vs git truth can diverge. Story 02 artifacts claimed `.pi/extensions/context-steward.ts`, but git history showed it landed later. Add a final committed-files verification step (manifest vs staged/committed files) before acceptance.

  - same session with evolving identifiers must converge to one canonical thread
  - failed reassociation/writes must not mutate persisted truth
  - duplicate replay must be idempotent
  - avoid fuzzy association unless explicitly specified
- File-backed persistence needs standard failure/concurrency injection coverage: partial writes, temp-write/rename failures, restart/index rebuild, and multi-instance races.
- Concurrency/source-order bugs are a real class: concurrent appends must preserve invocation order even if actor creation/duplicate checks/blocking work differ.

- Team logs and acceptance receipts should be generated from final artifacts/commit state automatically, since hand-maintained logs drifted.
- Tests should be labeled by confidence level (unit, service integration, fake runtime integration, real CLI/E2E, dogfood/manual), and story acceptance should require the appropriate level.

Overall durable takeaway: tighten the boundaries between accepted workspace state, committed repo state, and actual PI runtime behavior.

## Publish Epic / story sharding weaknesses

### 1. Story overload detection is not explicit enough

Some stories are broad but coherent; others are broad because too many concerns were bundled.

Track overload flags:

- multiple authority decisions
- multiple subsystem seams
- onboarding/import/recovery + steady-state
- core happy path + repair/recovery
- multiple different failure models
- source-truth + derived-state ownership in one story

Needed improvement:

```text
Add story shape review before publishing.
```

### 2. Missing “single governing idea” check

A story should have one conceptual center.

Good examples:

```text
Story 01: canonical thread/message store is source truth
Story 02: finalized PI activity becomes canonical messages
```

Weaker likely example:

```text
attach/import + path resolution + mapping + turn reconstruction + continuation + conflict handling
```

Needed improvement:

```text
For each story, require a one-sentence governing idea.
If weak, reconsider split.
```

### 3. Story archetypes are not formalized

Observed archetypes:

- foundation/invariant
- adapter/mapping
- semantic rule
- orchestration/convergence
- metadata/additive
- packaging/fixture
- repair/recovery

Needed improvement:

```text
Classify story type during publishing.
Use it as risk/scoping aid.
```

### 4. Onboarding/import/migration mixed with steady-state

Attach/import and migration behavior often has different invariants from normal runtime behavior.

Needed improvement:

```text
Warn when a story mixes steady-state with onboarding/import/migration/recovery.
Require justification or split.
```

### 5. Repair/recovery mixed with core happy path

Repair/recovery logic can introduce stale-state handling, partial failure semantics, and conflict rules.

Needed improvement:

```text
If repair/recovery is large enough to have separate invariants, consider a separate story.
```

### 6. Source-truth and derived-state authority boundaries need stronger sharding review

Stories that cross from canonical source records into derived state are risky.

Example:

```text
capture message + turn-state repair-needed marker
```

was okay because failure semantics were narrow.

But larger combinations may overload.

Needed improvement:

```text
Add authority-boundary review:
what owns truth before/after this story?
does this story change authority?
```

### 7. Future-feature boundaries should be preserved more systematically

Epic 1 did this well in places:

- records metadata only
- does not compile/reload
- turn lifecycle belongs to next story

Needed improvement:

```text
Add explicit future-feature boundary checklist in each story.
```

### 8. Integration path trace may be too user-flow focused

Coverage currently maps AC/TCs and critical user paths. But implementation failures often happen at production/runtime paths.

Needed improvement:

The concept was framed as an “Agentic AI Software Factory” in a deeper sense than “agents write code from tickets”: a pipeline for preserving and transforming intent across the full lifecycle, from idea/product intent into technical world, functional spec, story shards, enriched implementation packets, orchestrated builds, verification artifacts, commits, current-state docs, and process learning that improves the factory itself.

Key characteristics of the factory model:
- Each station has explicit inputs, outputs, authority boundaries, verification rules, handoff artifacts, and recovery points.
- Skills/roles are specialized workstations: product framing, architecture, epic writing, tech design, story publishing, enrichment, implementation, verification, quick fixes, epic review, and current-state regeneration.
- The system relies on durable work-in-progress artifacts (markdown specs, coverage maps, enriched stories, test plans, logs, envelopes, review notes, commits) so work is resumable and not dependent on agent memory.
- Quality gates exist at every transformation, not just at final test time, to catch coverage gaps, semantic drift, traceability issues, and artifact/commit mismatches.
- The process is intended to learn from itself: whether sharding caused friction, enrichment missed risks, verification is catching the right things, and whether enforcement should be CLI-based or skill-guided.

The discussion then confronted the risk that this could become overwrought. The conclusion was that the core idea is justified, but only for the right class of work: long context horizons, multiple agents, high ambiguity, complex domain decisions, many handoffs, expensive regressions, auditability, and work that spans days or weeks. For simpler work, the full pipeline would become process theater.

The recommended response was adaptive ceremony with multiple lanes:
- Lane 0: tiny fixes (issue → patch → test)
- Lane 1: bounded stories (enriched story → implement/verify)
- Lane 2: features/epics (epic → tech design → stories → orchestrated build)
- Lane 3: product/system work (PRD → architecture → epics → roadmap)

The full Liminal Spec pipeline was positioned as appropriate mainly for Lane 2/3 work. The main value is not more documentation, but making the transformations explicit and controllable: intent → requirements → design → story → code → tests → runtime.

The honest assessment was that the vision is broad, but not unreasonable for a durable agentic software factory. The open design challenge is deciding when each layer is necessary and how cheaply it can be skipped when it is not, with escape hatches and calibration to avoid overengineering. The PI Long Horizon project was called out as a strong fit because it is both a product problem (long-horizon agent context management) and a testbed for the factory process itself.

Here’s one common use case: an enterprise senior developer, tech lead, or staff engineer managing 4–6 software products, or 4–6 components of an interlocking product. Each component is its own self-contained, sizable chunk: CLI/SDK, front end, sophisticated data layer, API control surface. Alternatively, you might have 2–3 smaller applications, but a single experienced engineer could have 2 epics “baking” while shepherding specs for the next easy-bake epic. Each epic takes about 4–8 hours to implement if you don’t over-parallelize and you stick with the rigor. Once an epic is done baking, some amount of agent tag-teaming can tighten, verify, and polish it. So at any point, a single engineer has 4 epics in flight across 2–3 projects, or 1 large project with 3–5 scoped architectural tiers with clear contracts. That’s my rough vision for a product that is basically slow vibe for enterprise-targeted experienced software dev professionals.

[assistant]
{"text":"Yes — that use case makes the process feel much less overwrought.

You’re not targeting “generate a todo app from a prompt.” You’re targeting a senior engineer operating as a **multi-epic technical shepherd** across several serious systems.

The product shape is closer to:

> slow, rigorous vibe coding for enterprise engineers who need parallel leverage without losing architectural control.

## The user profile is key

Your target user is not a novice delegating everything.

It’s someone like:

- senior dev
- tech lead
- staff engineer
- platform/component owner
- experienced product engineer over multiple systems

They already know how to reason about architecture, tradeoffs, contracts, and risk. The tool gives them leverage without replacing their judgment.

## The working mode

The workflow you describe is something like:

```text
Engineer maintains 2–4 epics in flight.

Some are:
 being specified
 being technically designed
 being implemented by agents
 being verified/polished
 being closed out/current-documented

Engineer rotates attention:
 review spec
 correct architecture
 approve story shape
 let implementation bake
 inspect artifacts
 direct fixes
 accept/reject closeout
```

That is a very different mode from interactive pair programming.

It is closer to **technical portfolio management with agent execution loops**.

## “Slow vibe” is a good phrase

The vibe coding part is:

- you still shape intent conversationally,
- you still iterate with agents,
- you still get fast draft/build cycles.

The slow/enterprise part is:

- durable specs,
- traceability,
- test plans,
- verifier roles,
- artifact receipts,
- explicit gates,
- architecture preservation,
- cross-epic memory.

So:

```text
fast vibe = prompt -> code
slow vibe = intent -> durable spec -> bounded agent execution -> verified artifact
```

## Why the rigor is justified here

If one engineer has 4 epics in flight, memory becomes the bottleneck.

The process gives them:

- where each epic is,
- what was decided,
- what risks exist,
- what verifier found,
- what remains blocked,
- what can be resumed,
- what artifacts prove readiness.

That’s valuable. Without the structure, the engineer gets buried in transcripts, branches, half-finished PRs, and “what did the agent do again?” confusion.

## The factory metaphor fits

The engineer is not a factory worker. They are the **factory supervisor / architect / quality owner**.

Agents do:

- drafting,
- implementation,
- verification,
- quick fixes,
- current-state docs.

Engineer does:

- judgment,
- prioritization,
- architecture constraints,
- product decisions,
- acceptance,
- escalation.

## Product positioning

A possible concise positioning:

> Liminal Spec is a slow-vibe software factory for experienced engineers managing multiple serious epics. It turns architecture and requirements into durable, auditable agent work packets, then orchestrates implementation and verification without losing the thread.

## The core promise

Not:

```text
AI writes code faster
```

But:

```text
A senior engineer can safely keep more valuable work in motion.
```

That’s stronger and more enterprise-relevant.

## The design implication

The product needs lanes, as discussed:

- small fix lane
- story lane
- epic lane
- multi-project portfolio lane

For your target use case, the epic lane and portfolio lane are the differentiators.

The UI/CLI should probably help answer:

```text
What epics are baking?
Which need my judgment?
Which are blocked?
Which are ready for review?
Which artifacts changed?
Which verifier findings are unresolved?
What risks are being carried?
```

That’s the enterprise “slow vibe” cockpit.","textSignature":"{"v":1,"id":"msg_0e1fb8f5b5e7c000016a0cfed49f508196a78b2c14372e7282","phase":"final_answer"}"}

For larger products, there might also be a long-horizon product owner/BA. So any chunky project might have 1–3 long-horizon agents to hold the engineering and product knowledge.

detailed:
The product target was clarified as “slow vibe” for experienced enterprise engineers, not novice prompt-to-app generation. The primary user is a senior developer, tech lead, staff engineer, platform/component owner, or experienced product engineer who can manage multiple serious streams but needs leverage without losing architectural control.

The representative workload is one engineer keeping several epics moving in parallel: roughly 4 epics across 2–3 projects, or one large product split across 3–5 scoped tiers such as frontend, API/control surface, CLI/SDK, data layer, and infra/integration. Epics may “bake” for 4–8 hours under bounded agent execution, then go through tightening, verification, polish, and closeout. The value proposition is not simply faster coding; it is allowing a strong engineer to safely keep more valuable work in motion.

This positions the workflow as technical portfolio management with agent execution loops rather than interactive pair programming. The engineer rotates between reviewing specs, correcting architecture, approving story shape, letting agents implement, inspecting artifacts, directing fixes, and accepting or rejecting closeout. The product therefore needs a cockpit that shows what is baking, blocked, ready for review, awaiting human judgment, carrying risk, or holding unresolved verifier findings.

The rigor is justified by scale and memory limits. With 4 epics in flight or a 3–5-tier product, one human cannot keep all low-level details active. The process needs durable specs, traceability, test plans, verifier roles, artifact receipts, explicit gates, current-state docs, and cross-epic memory. The distinction became: fast vibe is prompt to code; slow vibe is intent to durable spec to bounded agent execution to verified artifact.

A key architectural direction emerged: use long-horizon role agents grounded in artifacts. The human acts as a quasi staff engineer, while tier-specific tech-lead agents hold local context for components or small apps. Larger products may also need a persistent product owner/BA agent for requirements continuity. A chunky project might have 1–3 long-horizon agents maintaining engineering and product knowledge.

The role model:
- Human senior/staff engineer owns judgment, prioritization, architecture coherence, tradeoffs, escalation, and acceptance.
- Tier tech-lead agents maintain component context, current-state docs, local constraints, prior decisions, and review specs against local reality.
- Product/BA agent maintains product flows, PRD/epic continuity, acceptance consistency, and detects requirement drift.
- Implementation and verifier agents execute story packets and independently check results.

Long-horizon agents must not rely on fuzzy transcript memory. They need stable source material: PRDs, epics, ADRs, tech designs, stories, test plans, current-state docs, implementation logs, verification receipts, explicit boundaries, and handoff artifacts. These documents form the shared memory and contract fabric across humans and agents.

The larger product direction is a role-based, long-horizon engineering cockpit spanning projects, epics, components/tiers, role agents, artifact graph, active implementation runs, verification status, unresolved decisions, risks, and current-state knowledge. The “bureaucracy” is not incidental; it is the coordination substrate that lets one human plus persistent agents manage systems larger than any single context window.

Liminal Spec target: senior/staff engineers or tech leads shepherding multiple serious epics/products, not novice prompt-to-app users.

Positioning: “slow vibe” enterprise software factory/cockpit. Promise is not faster codegen, but letting one experienced engineer safely keep more valuable work moving with architectural control, traceability, verification, and resumability.

Typical workload: 2–4 epics in flight across 2–3 projects, or one large product with 3–5 interlocking tiers/components. Every engineer starts as a tech lead and PO, working on one thing at a time, and still moves much faster than a typical team that would work on the same thing. Then, as they figure out the system, they build up long-horizon agents on each team and level up. Soon they are acting as principal engineer, principal architect, and PM, and managing 2–5 dev teams as you’d expect a principal engineer to do.

[assistant]
{"text":"Yes — that gives the adoption curve a lot of clarity.

The product is not asking users to start by managing an agentic software factory. It lets them **grow into one**.

## Adoption path

### Stage 1: Solo tech lead + PO on one epic

The engineer starts with one project/epic.

They use the system to:

- shape PRD / epic
- clarify architecture
- publish stories
- run implementation
- verify/closeout

At this stage, the human is both:

```text
tech lead + product owner + reviewer
```

Still much faster than a traditional team because agents do drafting, implementation, verification, and polish.

### Stage 2: Repeatable epic delivery

The engineer learns the pipeline and starts trusting artifacts.

They can now keep:

```text
one epic baking
one epic being specified
one epic being polished
```

They are still hands-on, but they are no longer linearly blocked.

### Stage 3: Role agents emerge

As the system grows, they instantiate long-horizon agents around components or functions:

- frontend tech lead agent
- API tech lead agent
- data/platform agent
- product/BA agent
- verification/release agent

These agents hold tier-specific context and maintain current-state docs.

### Stage 4: Human moves up a level

The human stops acting like one dev with helpers and starts acting like:

```text
principal engineer
principal architect
PM / product strategist
delivery lead
```

They coordinate multiple agentic “teams,” each with durable context and responsibilities.

### Stage 5: Multi-team orchestration

Eventually one experienced engineer can supervise:

```text
2–5 agentic dev teams
```

Each team has:

- specs
- current-state docs
- implementation runs
- verification loops
- role agents
- component ownership

The human manages:

- architecture coherence
- product priority
- cross-team contracts
- risk decisions
- final acceptance

## Why this is compelling

It mirrors normal career growth:

```text
developer -> tech lead -> staff/principal -> architect/PM-like coordination
```

But compresses the team structure into agentic roles.

So the product promise is not merely:

> do your current job faster

It is:

> let experienced engineers progressively operate at the next organizational level.

## Why the rigor still matters

The higher the user climbs, the more they need durable structure.

At Stage 1, rigor helps one epic stay clean.

At Stage 4, rigor is what prevents chaos across multiple agent teams.

Without artifacts, gates, current-state docs, and role boundaries, the system collapses into:

```text
many agents producing many plausible but uncoordinated outputs
```

With rigor, the human can supervise safely.","textSignature":"{"v":1,"id":"msg_0e1fb8f5b5e7c000016a0d002ec6908196ac235e6d1d8bcdc8","phase":"final_answer"}"}

You start as a 1-engineer team and grow into a multi-team software factory, carefully balancing the light and dark parts. Everyone wants a pure dark factory. I don’t think that’s what we want. I think we want a well-calibrated factory that is light where it needs to be and dark everywhere else.

[assistant]
{"text":"Yes — that framing is strong.

You start as:

```text
one engineer + one agentic process
```

and grow into:

```text
one engineer supervising a multi-team software factory
```

But the key design principle is not “maximize automation.” It is **calibrate light and dark**.

## Light vs dark factory

A pure dark factory means:

```text
spec -> agents -> code -> merge
```

with minimal human involvement.

That sounds attractive, but for serious software it is risky:

- silent requirement drift
- architecture erosion
- fake tests
- shallow verification
- unreviewed product decisions
- incoherent cross-team contracts
- agents optimizing for completion instead of correctness

For enterprise/high-value systems, that is not the right target.

## The calibrated factory

Your model is more like:

```text
dark where work is bounded and verifiable
light where judgment, taste, risk, or authority matter
```

### Dark zones

Good candidates for dark/mostly-dark automation:

- drafting from clear source artifacts
- boilerplate implementation
- test generation from explicit TCs
- mechanical refactors
- fixture construction
- verification passes
- artifact summarization
- current-state doc generation
- bounded quick fixes

### Light zones

Human-in-the-loop zones:

- product intent
- architecture boundaries
- story sharding judgment
- build strategy selection/override
- risk acceptance
- cross-tier contract decisions
- verifier disagreement
- release/merge decisions
- ambiguous customer/product tradeoffs

## Why this matters

The goal is not to remove the engineer.

The goal is to move the engineer to the highest-leverage points:

```text
decide
shape
review
accept
coordinate
escalate
```

while agents handle the bounded work.

That is much more plausible than a pure dark factory.

## The product challenge

The product has to know when to be light.

It needs escalation surfaces:

- “This story is overloaded; split?”
- “Verifier found product ambiguity.”
- “Production path not proven.”
- “Artifact and git disagree.”
- “Runtime contract assumption unvalidated.”
- “Gate passed but ran zero E2E tests.”
- “Two tier agents disagree on API contract.”

And it needs dark automation where confidence is high:

- “Story 03 passed staged verification.”
- “All TCs mapped.”
- “No risk reminders unresolved.”
- “Commit matches final package.”
- “Current-state docs regenerated.”

## Great positioning phrase

> Start as a one-engineer team. Grow into a calibrated multi-team software factory.

Or:

> Not a dark factory — a calibrated factory: light where judgment matters, dark where work is bounded.

That feels like the core philosophy.","textSignature":"{"v":1,"id":"msg_0e1fb8f5b5e7c000016a0d0076808c819684172a10f7950502","phase":"final_answer"}"}
detailed:
The thread sharpened the product narrative as a growth path: an engineer starts as a solo tech lead + PO on one epic, using agents to draft PRDs/architecture, publish stories, implement, verify, and close out work faster than a traditional team. As they trust the pipeline, they can run multiple epics in parallel (one baking, one specifying, one polishing), then introduce durable role agents around components/functions (frontend, API, data/platform, product/BA, verification/release). At that point the human is no longer acting like one dev with helpers; they become a principal engineer / principal architect / PM / delivery lead coordinating 2–5 agentic dev teams with shared specs, current-state docs, verification loops, and ownership boundaries.

A second framing clarified the factory model: the goal is not a pure “dark factory” where spec → agents → code → merge happens with minimal human involvement. That is seen as risky for serious software because it can cause requirement drift, architecture erosion, fake tests, shallow verification, poor contract handling, and unreviewed product decisions. Instead, the desired product is a calibrated factory: dark where work is bounded and verifiable, light where judgment, taste, risk, or authority matter.

The division is explicit:
- Dark/mostly-dark: drafting from clear artifacts, boilerplate implementation, test generation from explicit cases, mechanical refactors, fixtures, verification passes, artifact summarization, current-state doc regeneration, bounded quick fixes.
- Light/human-in-loop: product intent, architecture boundaries, sharding judgment, build strategy, risk acceptance, cross-tier contracts, verifier disagreements, release/merge decisions, ambiguous tradeoffs.

The product implication is that it must support escalation and confidence surfaces (e.g. overloaded story, product ambiguity, unproven production path, artifact/git mismatch, unvalidated runtime assumptions, passed gate with zero E2E tests, cross-tier API disagreement) while also automating confidently when evidence is strong (e.g. staged verification passed, all test cases mapped, no unresolved risk reminders, commit matches package, docs regenerated).

Core positioning that emerged: “Start as a one-engineer team. Grow into a calibrated multi-team software factory.”
brief:
Core framing: users grow from a single engineer running one epic to a principal-level operator supervising 2–5 agentic dev teams. The product should support an adoption curve: solo tech lead/PO → repeatable epic delivery → role agents around components → human operating at architect/PM/delivery-lead level → multi-team orchestration.

Key principle: not a pure “dark factory,” but a calibrated one. Go dark for bounded, verifiable work (drafting, boilerplate implementation, test generation, refactors, doc generation, closed-loop verification) and stay light where judgment/risk/authority matter (product intent, architecture, prioritization, contract decisions, ambiguity, merge/release acceptance).

Need strong escalation surfaces for ambiguity, disagreement, contract drift, insufficient verification, or overloaded stories; use automation when confidence is high.

Its central idea is not “write more docs.” It is:

Each stage creates a more implementation-ready projection of the previous stage while keeping traceability.

## `ls-prd`

Purpose: product-level requirements and proto-epics.

It captures:

- product vision
- target users
- key workflows
- features as proto-epics
- scenario-driven acceptance criteria
- rough architecture summary
- sequencing/milestones
- scope boundaries

Purpose: establish the technical world.

It defines:

- architecture thesis
- stack choices
- system shape
- ownership boundaries
- runtime/deployment model
- cross-cutting concerns
- data/control flows
- integration boundaries
- nonfunctional constraints

It gives downstream specs a stable technical frame so every epic/story does not rediscover architecture from scratch.

---

## `ls-epic`

Purpose: turn a PRD feature into a full functional spec.

It is an execution contract, not just a description.

Typical chain:

```text
user/workflow
 -> flows
 -> acceptance criteria
 -> test conditions
 -> data contracts
 -> tech-design questions
 -> story breakdown
```

Key strengths:

- ACs and TCs co-located
- functional behavior separated from implementation design
- data contracts allowed but stack-neutral
- unresolved tech questions made explicit
- stories trace back to AC/TC coverage
- reduces agent invention during implementation

Epic 1 was a strong example: canonical Thread, messages, typed parts, prompt-bounded turns, attach/import, repair, and fixtures.

Purpose: translate an epic into implementable technical design and test plan.

- what interfaces/contracts are needed
- what schemas/storage records exist
- how flows execute
- what failure/degraded states exist
- what tests map to which ACs/TCs
- what implementation sequence should be used

- should explicitly model source/derived atomicity
- should call out runtime/command propagation
- should specify cache invalidation/session switching
- should separate service behavior from real runtime path
- should identify production/e2e seams early

Purpose: shard a detailed epic into implementation stories.

- summary/description
- user profile/context
- story-scoped ACs/TCs
- source references
- verification gates
- definition of done
- Jira-friendly markers
- coverage mapping

- one governing idea
- story archetype
- overload flags
- authority boundaries
- lifecycle mixing
- repair/import/steady-state separation
- future-feature boundaries

- implementation targets

- build strategy guidance

brief:
- Liminal Spec is an artifact-driven pipeline for preserving intent through transformations: `ls-prd → ls-arch → ls-epic → ls-tech-design/test-plan → ls-publish-epic → ls-enrich → ls-impl/lbuild-impl → closeout`.
- Stage roles: PRD = product/users/workflows/scope; arch = system/runtime/boundaries; epic = execution contract with ACs/TCs, data contracts, open tech questions; tech-design = modules/interfaces/schemas/flows/failures/tests; publish-epic = story sharding with story-shape judgment; enrich = implementation/runtime/build/risk context.
- `ls-impl` is the orchestration loop: validate → implement → verify → fix → package → review → commit; `status=ok` is not enough without durable repo truth.
- `lbuild-impl` is the resumable, auditable CLI/runtime that executes `ls-impl`.
- Key lesson: most failures come from boundary drift (spec→story, source→derived state, code→runtime, tests→real behavior, receipts→repo truth). Goal is a calibrated agentic factory: bounded/verifiable work automated, human judgment stays on architecture/risk/product authority.

Summarize each story in Epic One and how implementation went.

[assistant]
{"text":"## Epic 1: Session Context Store

Epic 1 built the canonical source substrate for PI Long Horizon.

```text
canonical Thread
 -> messages/parts
 -> prompt-bounded turns
 -> live PI capture
 -> generated-session metadata
 -> attach/import
 -> repair
 -> fixtures
```

## Story 00: Foundation

Established shared scaffolding:

- domain vocabulary
- constants
- error/result helpers
- ID/fingerprint helpers
- test scaffolding
- verification scripts

Implementation went cleanly. It mostly avoided feature behavior, which was correct. Verifier found small contract issues around target-key/fixture-builder behavior; quick fixes handled them.

**Takeaway:** good foundation story; process worked with low churn.

---

## Story 01: Thread, Actor, Message, And Part Store

Built the durable canonical store:

- thread creation/opening
- target metadata
- schema gating
- actor declarations
- append-only messages
- canonical ordering

This was the first hard persistence story. Verifier found serious issues:

- alias/session identity duplication
- unsafe fuzzy `cwd` matching
- failed reassociation mutating disk
- failed create leaving partial threads
- cross-instance write races
- source-order inversion under concurrency

Fixes hardened the canonical substrate.

**Takeaway:** difficult but successful. Validated the need for strong verification.

---

## Story 02: Live PI Activity Capture

Mapped finalized PI runtime activity into canonical messages:

- user prompts
- assistant responses
- tool results
- runtime notes
- duplicate detection
- append failure reporting
- repair-needed turn state on partial failure

Initial implementation built service/mapping logic but missed enough of the real PI extension path.

Verifier caught:

- missing `message_end` production/runtime hook
- runtime lifecycle notes not routed
- service tests proving helpers but not actual extension behavior

Later work added stronger E2E around the real extension path.

**Takeaway:** exposed “service works but runtime path not wired” as a recurring process risk.

---

## Story 03: Prompt-Bounded Turn Lifecycle

Grouped captured messages into canonical turns:

- prompt starts a turn
- assistant/tool cycles stay in the turn
- turn open/closed lifecycle
- pre-turn/source-record reporting
- repair-needed state when derived turn write fails

Key issue: adding derived turn state changed the atomicity boundary. Source append alone was not enough; source + derived turn updates needed careful serialization/failure behavior.

**Takeaway:** source truth plus derived state needs explicit atomicity/failure semantics.

---

## Story 04: Generated Session Metadata

Added metadata for generated PI session/projection state:

- generated file path
- projection revision information
- target metadata
- active generated session bookkeeping

This was narrower and cleaner than Story 03. It clarified that generated PI sessions are derived artifacts, not source truth.

**Takeaway:** good small metadata story; reinforced canonical-vs-derived boundary.

---

## Story 05: Attach And Import Existing PI Sessions

Imported unmanaged PI sessions into canonical Thread state:

- attach to existing PI session
- import active linear path
- preserve metadata
- reconstruct turns
- continue live capture afterward

This was coherent but risky because it mixed onboarding/import with steady-state continuation.

Issues centered on transition state:

- import metadata
- active branch/path context
- continuation after attach
- partial import/failure state
- avoiding polluted canonical truth

**Takeaway:** attach/import stories need explicit transition-state atomicity and steady-state handoff checks.

---

## Story 06: Turn Health And Repair

Detected and repaired missing/incomplete turn state:

- health checks
- reconstruct prompt-bounded turns from messages
- block downstream maintenance until valid
- repair stale/incomplete turn records

This story was more about readiness contracts and repair semantics than visible user behavior.

It seemed relatively clean, but highlighted that “ready” has to mean something precise for downstream smoothing/chunking/projection.

**Takeaway:** repair/readiness is core infrastructure, not optional cleanup.

---

## Story 07: Real-Session Fixtures

Created Thread-shaped fixtures from real managed Threads or PI sessions:

- preserve canonical ordering
- typed parts
- repair status
- fixture metadata
- command/runtime fixture surfaces

This acted as a capstone integration story. It exposed hidden cross-story runtime assumptions, especially around:

- command context propagation
- extension cache/session switching
- active branch/path metadata
- artifact-vs-git mismatch
- E2E coverage gaps

**Takeaway:** fixture/capstone stories are not just packaging; they pressure-test the whole feature.

---

## Overall Epic 1 implementation assessment

Epic 1 went well, but not trivially.

The spec was strong, and the implementation process caught real issues. The biggest recurring weaknesses were boundary problems:

```text
service code vs real runtime path
workspace artifact vs committed git truth
source state vs derived state
import transition vs steady-state continuation
unit tests vs E2E behavior
```

The process worked because verifiers and artifacts surfaced those issues before they became invisible architectural debt.","textSignature":"{"v":1,"id":"msg_0e5ce52fa8cb3f22016a0d16c7470c819585705d0bceaa491a","phase":"final_answer"}"}
detailed:
Epic 1 built the canonical source substrate for PI Long Horizon: threads/messages/parts, prompt-bounded turns, live PI capture, generated-session metadata, attach/import, repair, and real-session fixtures.

- Story 00, Foundation: added shared vocabulary, constants, errors/results, ID/fingerprint helpers, tests, and verification scripts. Implementation was clean; verifier only found minor target-key/fixture-builder contract issues.

- Story 01, Thread/Actor/Message/Part store: implemented durable canonical persistence: thread creation/opening, target metadata, schema gating, actors, append-only messages, and ordering. This was the first difficult story. Verification exposed serious persistence risks: identity duplication, unsafe fuzzy cwd matching, partial disk mutation on failed operations, cross-instance races, and ordering inversion. Fixes hardened the substrate.

- Story 02, Live PI activity capture: mapped finalized runtime activity into canonical messages for prompts, responses, tool results, notes, duplicate detection, append failure reporting, and repair-needed state. Initial work covered service/mapping logic but missed real PI extension wiring. Verifier caught missing `message_end`, lifecycle note routing gaps, and insufficient runtime/E2E coverage.

- Story 03, Prompt-bounded turn lifecycle: grouped messages into turns with open/closed lifecycle and repair semantics. Main issue was atomicity: once derived turn state existed, source message append alone was insufficient; source and derived updates needed explicit serialization and failure handling.

- Story 04, Generated session metadata: added generated path, projection revision, target metadata, and active generated-session bookkeeping. This was narrower and cleaner, reinforcing that generated sessions are derived artifacts, not canonical truth.

- Story 05, Attach/import existing PI sessions: imported unmanaged sessions into canonical thread state, preserving metadata, reconstructing turns, and resuming live capture. Main risk was mixing onboarding/import with steady-state continuation; transition atomicity, active branch/path context, and partial-failure handling were key concerns.

- Story 06, Turn health and repair: added health checks, turn reconstruction from messages, downstream blocking until valid, and stale/incomplete turn repair. It clarified that “ready” must be precise for later maintenance/projection work.

- Story 07, Real-session fixtures: generated thread-shaped fixtures from real managed threads/PI sessions, preserving ordering, typed parts, repair status, and metadata. As a capstone, it exposed hidden assumptions around command context propagation, cache/session switching, active branch/path metadata, artifact-vs-git truth, and E2E gaps.

Overall, Epic 1 succeeded but was nontrivial. The spec and verification process caught real defects. Recurring risk areas were boundary mismatches: service vs runtime path, workspace artifact vs committed git truth, source vs derived state, import transition vs steady state, and unit tests vs E2E behavior.
